ConsensusMetaDA: an R Package for consensus-based differential abundance analysis of metagenomic data.

Manoharan Kumar, Matt Field

Last modified: 2026-09-01. Compiled: 2026-09-09

1 Introduction to ConsensusMetaDA

ConsensusMetaDA is an R package for microbiome differential abundance (DA) analysis using multiple algorithms and reaching a consensus. No single tool performs best on all metagenomic datasets, so a consensus approach yields more robust differentially abundant taxa. ConsensusMetaDA runs seven widely used tools — edgeR, DESeq2, ALDEx2, metagenomeSeq, ADAPT, ANCOM-BC2, and MaAsLin3 — takes standard biom + sample table input, and also produces microbiome visualisations (alpha diversity, beta diversity, rarefaction, bidirectional and scaled plots).

Consensus is reached three ways: vote rules (union / k-of-7 / intersect), p-value combination (Fisher, Stouffer, and the dependence-robust Cauchy/ACAT), and rank-sum aggregation.

ConsensusMetaDA is organised around two core functions:

  • build_OTU_counts() — build (or filter) a phyloseq object from a biom file + sample table (+ optional taxonomy), or from an existing phyloseq object.
  • OTUs_multi_DA() — perform DA analysis across all pairwise comparisons.

Plotting is provided by OTUs_plots().

# ADAPT requires R >= 4.4 (use R 4.4.2)
# if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
# for (pkg in c("phyloseq","DESeq2","ALDEx2","edgeR","metagenomeSeq","ANCOMBC"))
#   if (!require(pkg, character.only = TRUE)) BiocManager::install(pkg)
# # ADAPT, maaslin3 as per their install instructions
# if (!require("ConsensusMetaDA", quietly = TRUE)) {
#   if (!require("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("remotes")
#   remotes::install_github("kmanoharan01/ConsensusMetaDA")
# }

1.1 Load libraries

library(ggplot2)
library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)
library(ConsensusMetaDA)

2 Example data

We use the bundled ecc_saliva dataset (early-childhood-caries saliva microbiome). It is available both as example files under inst/extdata/ and as a ready-made phyloseq object via data().

library(ADAPT)
data("ecc_saliva")
ecc_saliva
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 280 taxa and 161 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 161 samples by 2 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 280 taxa by 7 taxonomic ranks ]
## refseq()      DNAStringSet:      [ 280 reference sequences ]
# resolve bundled example files (works regardless of working directory)
ecc_saliva_biom         <- system.file("extdata", "ecc_saliva_Otu.biom",
                                        package = "ConsensusMetaDA")
ecc_saliva_sample_table <- system.file("extdata", "ecc_saliva_sample_table.txt",
                                        package = "ConsensusMetaDA")

# taxonomy taken from the bundled object so it matches the biom's ASV ids
ecc_saliva_tax <- tax_table(ecc_saliva)

3 Building a phyloseq object

build_OTU_counts() has two entry points and optional filters (abundance_threshold, prevalence_threshold, rarity_threshold, variance_threshold). Because the first argument is now physeq, always call it with named arguments.

3.1 From files (biom + sample table + taxonomy)

ecc_saliva_build_OTU_counts <- build_OTU_counts(
  biom                 = ecc_saliva_biom,
  sample_table         = ecc_saliva_sample_table,
  tax_tables           = ecc_saliva_tax,
  abundance_threshold  = 10,
  prevalence_threshold = 0.1,
  rarity_threshold     = 0,
  variance_threshold   = 0
)
ecc_saliva_build_OTU_counts
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 114 taxa and 161 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 161 samples by 3 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 114 taxa by 7 taxonomic ranks ]

3.2 From a prebuilt phyloseq object

When you already have a phyloseq object, pass it via physeq = and use the function purely for filtering. This is orientation-safe (it transposes internally when taxa are stored as columns).

ecc_ps <- build_OTU_counts(physeq = ecc_saliva, prevalence_threshold = 0.1)
ecc_ps
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 114 taxa and 161 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 161 samples by 2 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 114 taxa by 7 taxonomic ranks ]
## refseq()      DNAStringSet:      [ 114 reference sequences ]

3.3 Individual filters

Each filter can be used on its own.

build_OTU_counts(biom = ecc_saliva_biom, sample_table = ecc_saliva_sample_table,
                 tax_tables = ecc_saliva_tax, rarity_threshold = 0.1)
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 244 taxa and 161 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 161 samples by 3 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 244 taxa by 7 taxonomic ranks ]
build_OTU_counts(biom = ecc_saliva_biom, sample_table = ecc_saliva_sample_table,
                 tax_tables = ecc_saliva_tax, abundance_threshold = 10)
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 238 taxa and 161 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 161 samples by 3 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 238 taxa by 7 taxonomic ranks ]
build_OTU_counts(biom = ecc_saliva_biom, sample_table = ecc_saliva_sample_table,
                 tax_tables = ecc_saliva_tax, prevalence_threshold = 0.1)
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 114 taxa and 161 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 161 samples by 3 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 114 taxa by 7 taxonomic ranks ]
build_OTU_counts(biom = ecc_saliva_biom, sample_table = ecc_saliva_sample_table,
                 tax_tables = ecc_saliva_tax, variance_threshold = 0.2)
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 241 taxa and 161 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 161 samples by 3 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 241 taxa by 7 taxonomic ranks ]

4 Performing differential abundance

OTUs_multi_DA() runs the seven tools on every pairwise comparison of the grouping variable (default group_var = "Group") and consolidates the results. An UpSet plot is written per comparison.

ecc_saliva_DA <- OTUs_multi_DA(ecc_saliva_build_OTU_counts,
                               group_var = "Group", fdr_cut = 0.05)
## Choose 'Control' as the baseline condition
## 114 taxa and 161 samples being analyzed...
## Selecting Reference Set... 28 taxa selected as reference
## 25 differentially abundant taxa detected
## Differential abundance analysis for Group (Case VS Control)
## 114 taxa and 161 samples analyzed
## 28 taxa are selected as reference and 25 taxa are differentially abundant
## 
## --------------------------------------------------
##   Consensus summary - Case_vs_Control  (FDR < 0.05)
## --------------------------------------------------
##   Tools that ran      : 7
##   Total taxa tested   : 114
## 
##   Taxa significant by N tools:
##     1/7 tools : 37
##     2/7 tools : 16
##     3/7 tools : 4
##     4/7 tools : 3
##     5/7 tools : 4
##     6/7 tools : 2
##     7/7 tools : 1
## 
##   Consensus tiers (vote rules):
##     Any tool (>=1)          : 67
##     Majority (>=4)          : 10
##     Strict (>=6, all-but-1) : 3
##     Unanimous (7/7)        : 1
## 
##   Combined-p methods:
##     Fisher                    : 58
##     Stouffer                  : 56
##     Cauchy (dependence-robust): 50
## --------------------------------------------------
names(ecc_saliva_DA)                     # the contrasts that were run
## [1] "Case_vs_Control"
cons <- ecc_saliva_DA[[1]]$consolidated  # consolidated table for first contrast

4.1 The consolidated table

For each taxon the consolidated table carries, per tool, a log fold-change, p-value, adjusted p-value and significance flag, plus:

  • n_sig — how many of the seven tools called the taxon significant
  • n_tools — how many tools ran
  • combined p-values (appended automatically):
    • p_fisher, padj_fisher, sig_fisher
    • p_stouffer, padj_stouffer, sig_stouffer
    • p_cauchy, padj_cauchy, sig_cauchy

Because the seven tools share the same count matrix and overlapping models (i.e. their p-values are correlated), the Cauchy (ACAT) combiner is recommended — it is valid under arbitrary dependence. Fisher and Stouffer assume independence and are provided as comparators.

grep("fisher|stouffer|cauchy", names(cons), value = TRUE)
## [1] "p_fisher"      "padj_fisher"   "sig_fisher"    "p_stouffer"    "padj_stouffer" "sig_stouffer"  "p_cauchy"      "padj_cauchy"   "sig_cauchy"

There is deliberately no composite fold-change column: the tools report fold-change on different footings (ALDEx2’s effect is a standardized effect size, not a log2 fold-change; ANCOM-BC2 / MaAsLin3 / metaSeq each carry their own normalization), so averaging them would mix different quantities. Read each tool’s logFC_<tool> column directly if needed.

4.2 Consensus decision rules

compare_decision_rules() puts every strategy side by side — vote rules, the three combiners, and rank-sum aggregation.

compare_decision_rules(cons, fdr_cut = 0.05)
##                                   rule      method votes n_called
## 1                       Union (1 of 7)        vote     1       67
## 2                               2 of 7        vote     2       30
## 3                               3 of 7        vote     3       14
## 4                               4 of 7        vote     4       10
## 5                               5 of 7        vote     5        7
## 6                               6 of 7        vote     6        3
## 7                   Intersect (7 of 7)        vote     7        1
## 8                      Fisher combined combination    NA       58
## 9                    Stouffer combined combination    NA       56
## 10 Cauchy combined (dependence-robust) combination    NA       50
## 11                Rank-sum aggregation combination    NA       14

4.3 Compact summary table

build_summary_table() gives per-tool adjusted p-values and ranks, the rank-sum, and the order-statistic p-values p_union / p_atleast2 / p_intersect_all. Threshold p_union for the union, p_intersect_all for the intersect, and use p_atleast_k() for any k.

st <- build_summary_table(cons)
st$p_atleast5 <- p_atleast_k(st, k = 5)   # "at least 5 of 7 tools" p-value
head(st)

describe_summary_table()                  # column dictionary
##            column                               description                                                                      detail
## 1    <tool>_adj_p                          Per-tool p-value                                          BH-adjusted p-value from that tool
## 2     <tool>_rank Rank of the p-value reported by that tool                      Smallest rank = most significant reported by that tool
## 3        rank_sum                              Sum of ranks                    Sum of every <tool>_rank column. Table is sorted by this
## 4         p_union        Smallest adjusted p-value observed          Threshold for the UNION: p_union < cutoff means >=1 tool called it
## 5      p_atleast2    2nd-smallest adjusted p-value observed Threshold for AT LEAST 2 tools. Use p_atleast_k(summary_tab, k) for other k
## 6 p_intersect_all         Largest adjusted p-value observed                           Threshold for the INTERSECT: every tool called it

The summary-table columns are:

  • <tool>_adj_p — BH-adjusted p-value from each tool
  • <tool>_rank — rank of that tool’s p-value (smallest = most significant)
  • rank_sum — sum of the per-tool ranks (table is sorted by this)
  • p_union — smallest adjusted p-value across tools (threshold → union)
  • p_atleast2 — 2nd-smallest (threshold → “≥2 tools”); p_atleast_k() for other k
  • p_intersect_all — largest adjusted p-value (threshold → intersect)

5 Plotting functions

OTUs_plots() creates five plots — (1) alpha diversity (Shannon), (2) beta diversity (PCoA), (3) rarefaction curve, (4) scaled taxa-level plot and (5) bidirectional plots — and saves them as PDFs. It also returns them as objects for inline display. See ?OTUs_plots.

ecc_saliva_plots <- OTUs_plots(ecc_saliva_build_OTU_counts)
## Running comparison: Control_vs_Case 
## Processing: Phylum for Control vs Case
## Completed: Phylum for Control vs Case 
## Processing: Class for Control vs Case
## Completed: Class for Control vs Case 
## Processing: Order for Control vs Case
## Completed: Order for Control vs Case 
## Processing: Family for Control vs Case
## Completed: Family for Control vs Case 
## Processing: Genus for Control vs Case
## Completed: Genus for Control vs Case 
## Running comparison: Case_vs_Control 
## Processing: Phylum for Case vs Control
## Completed: Phylum for Case vs Control 
## Processing: Class for Case vs Control
## Completed: Class for Case vs Control 
## Processing: Order for Case vs Control
## Completed: Order for Case vs Control 
## Processing: Family for Case vs Control
## Completed: Family for Case vs Control 
## Processing: Genus for Case vs Control
## Completed: Genus for Case vs Control

5.1 Rarefaction curve

A rarefaction curve shows how many species you detect as sequencing depth increases, allowing fair comparison of diversity across samples sequenced to different depths.

5.2 Alpha diversity

Alpha diversity (Shannon index) measures within-sample richness and evenness.

print(ecc_saliva_plots$AlphaDiv$tax_level)

5.3 Beta diversity / PCoA

Beta diversity (principal coordinates analysis) shows how microbiome composition differs among groups and samples.

print(ecc_saliva_plots$BetaDiv)

5.4 Bidirectional plot

A bidirectional plot shows two groups’ mean abundance and prevalence together, richer than either alone.

print(ecc_saliva_plots$all_comparisons_results$Control_vs_Case$Genus_plot)

Interpretation:

  • High abundance + high prevalence — beneficial bacteria expanding
  • Higher abundance + lower prevalence — pathogen blooming in some individuals
  • Lower abundance + higher prevalence — opportunists colonising stressed communities
  • Lower abundance + lower prevalence — sensitive bacteria dying off

6 Citing ConsensusMetaDA

When using this package, please cite ConsensusMetaDA and every method used.

citation("ConsensusMetaDA")

DA tools

  • DESeq2 — Love, M.I., Huber, W., Anders, S. (2014). Moderated estimation of fold change and dispersion for RNA-seq data with DESeq2. Genome Biology 15(12):550.
  • edgeR — Robinson MD, McCarthy DJ, Smyth GK (2010). Bioinformatics 26, 139–140. McCarthy DJ, Chen Y, Smyth GK (2012). Nucleic Acids Research 40, 4288–4297.
  • ALDEx2 — Fernandes, A.D. et al. (2013). ANOVA-Like Differential Expression (ALDEx) Analysis for Mixed Population RNA-Seq. PLOS ONE 8(7), e67019.
  • ADAPT — Wang, M., Fontaine, S., Jiang, H., Li, G. (2024). ADAPT: Analysis of Microbiome Differential Abundance by Pooling Tobit Models. Bioinformatics 40(11).
  • metagenomeSeq — Paulson JN, Stine OC, Bravo HC, Pop M (2013). Differential abundance analysis for microbial marker-gene surveys. Nature Methods 10, 1200–1202.
  • ANCOM-BC2 — Lin, H., Peddada, S.D. (2020). Analysis of compositions of microbiomes with bias correction. Nature Communications 11, 3514.
  • MaAsLin — Mallick, H. et al. (2021). Multivariable association discovery in population-scale meta-omics studies. PLoS Computational Biology 17(11), e1009442.

Consensus / combination methods

  • Cauchy combination (recommended) — Liu, Y., Xie, J. (2020). Cauchy combination test: a powerful test with analytic p-value calculation under arbitrary dependency structures. JASA 115(529), 393–402.
  • ACAT — Liu, Y. et al. (2019). ACAT: a fast and powerful p-value combination method for rare-variant analysis. AJHG 104(3), 410–421.
  • Fisher’s method — Fisher, R.A. (1932). Statistical Methods for Research Workers, 4th ed. Oliver and Boyd.
  • Stouffer’s Z — Stouffer, S.A. et al. (1949). The American Soldier, Vol. 1. Princeton University Press.
  • Rank aggregation — Guo, Zhao, Ye, Sheng, Shyr (2014).

Framework

  • phyloseq — McMurdie, P.J., Holmes, S. (2013). phyloseq: an R package for reproducible interactive analysis and graphics of microbiome census data. PLOS ONE 8(4), e61217. ```
